text: The most common load-testing failure isn't a missing tool or a misconfigured script — it's testing the wrong thing entirely. A test built around unrealistic traffic can pass cleanly in staging and still leave the real system falling over in production, because the test never exercised anything close to how production traffic actually behaves.

Here's the mistake in its purest form: firing an identical request at a single endpoint, as fast as possible, forever. That measures how quickly one perfectly cacheable, perfectly uniform code path can be hammered. It does not measure how your system behaves under the mixed, skewed, bursty traffic a real production system actually receives — and that gap is exactly why a passing load test and a production outage can both be true at once.

A realistic test reproduces four things pulled from real production data rather than invented in the test script. The request mix — the real relative frequency of endpoints, from access logs or APM traces. Think time — the pause real users take between actions, which changes how connection pools and rate limiters actually behave. Session correlation — a real sequence of related requests per simulated user, not independent one-off calls. And data variety — a spread of cache and database keys, not the same hot record requested over and over.

In practice that means weighting your virtual users the way real traffic is actually weighted: most of it product-page views, a smaller share cart updates, a small slice actual checkout and payment, each with think time pulled from real session data — not an equal split across every endpoint you happen to know about.

How load arrives matters as much as how much arrives. An instant ramp to peak tests whether autoscaling and connection pools absorb a sudden spike. A soak test — steady realistic load sustained for hours, not minutes — catches an entirely different class of failure: memory leaks, connection pool exhaustion, log disk fill-up, and certificate or token expiry that only show up after sustained operation.

Run that way, a load test's result is a real go or no-go signal — latency percentiles, error rate, and resource utilization at your forecasted peak, worth fixing before a real event rather than discovering live. Next lesson turns this same rigor into an ongoing discipline: performance engineering as something you practice continuously, not something you only reach for once users start complaining.
